newsitem.title: UK: German data spell trouble for European bonds.
newsitem.headline: German data spell trouble for European bonds.

text.p: German data showing economic recovery more robust than expected has weakened prospects for interest rate cuts and could point to trouble ahead for the recent rally in European bonds, analysts said on Wednesday.
"This data clearly rules out rate cuts in Germany and makes the Bund market even more vulnerable," said Teis Knuthsen, director of European analysis at First Chicago.
Wednesday's economic data, covering gross domestic product and industrial orders, helped to dampen recent talk about the chances of a German-led round of European interest rate cuts.
Knuthsen said that what he called a liquidity-driven rally in most world bond markets over the last couple of weeks "may continue for a while but looks increasingly stretched".

"There is no relative value at all in core European markets given that yields have declined dramatically and most yield spreads have narrowed, so risk premiums have come down a lot almost everywhere," he said.

With bonds from countries like France and the Netherlands trading below Germany on 10-year yield spreads, Knuthsen said significant numbers of investors might be tempted soon to move out of bonds altogether in the search for better rewards.
This could be the case for those who believed there would be higher global growth in 1997.
Investors would have to think growth would continue to slow to justify putting money into U.S. Treasuries, and Knuthsen said he did not think this would be the case.

And the European high-yielding bonds were not a desirable haven because their spreads against Bunds were too narrow as markets "closed their eyes to political risk in Italy and overrated the chances they would join European Economic and Monetary Union in 1999".
Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets, forecast a "quite significant correction" in early 1997 in both Bunds and U.S. Treasuries after the end-year bull market faded.
New German debt supply at the beginning of 1997 in the 10 and possibly 30 year sectors could combine with a U.S. Treasury sell-off to push Bund yields back up to six percent, she said.
The benchmark 10-year Bund was quoted at 104.15, yielding 5.657 percent in afternoon European trade.
Core European markets should move in tandem with Germany, she said, adding that it would take something like a 40 basis point sell-off in Bunds to open up "a tiny bit of widening on core spreads".
Lifton cautioned that Bund prices had not been reacting to fundamentals in their recent outperformance since yields had been falling despite a consensus belief that the economy was recovering.

Tuesday's data showing industrial output fell 1.8 percent in October helped German debt prices, but this was offset on Wednesday by news German gross domestic product rose 1.0 percent in the third quarter and industrial orders rose 2.9 percent in October. Forecasts had been for 0.9 percent and 0.8 percent respectively.
Michael Lewis, senior economist at London Bond Broking, said the latest data suggested there was still momentum in the German economy, and there was no expectation of lower repo rates.
Lewis said the market might well test the all-time yield low around 5.535 percent, but yields should start backing up to the 5.80-90 percent level over the next three months.
